claim: Sepsis affects 1.7 million Americans yearly.
source: Sepsis poses both a significant health concern, affecting 1.7 million and killing 270,000 Americans yearly, and economic burden (> $20 billion annually) (CDC, 2020).
evidence: Cited from CDC, 2020 reference

claim: Sepsis kills 270,000 Americans yearly.
source: Sepsis poses both a significant health concern, affecting 1.7 million and killing 270,000 Americans yearly, and economic burden (> $20 billion annually) (CDC, 2020).
evidence: Cited from CDC, 2020 reference

claim: Sepsis poses an economic burden of more than $20 billion annually.
source: Sepsis poses both a significant health concern, affecting 1.7 million and killing 270,000 Americans yearly, and economic burden (> $20 billion annually) (CDC, 2020).
evidence: Cited from CDC, 2020 reference

claim: Sepsis is characterized by cytokine storm, a maladaptive response to a mismanaged infection.
source: Sepsis is characterized by cytokine storm, a maladaptive response to a mismanaged infection, that is comprised of both pro- and anti-inflammatory cytokines.
evidence: Statement based on established understanding of sepsis pathophysiology

claim: Cytokine storm in sepsis is comprised of both pro- and anti-inflammatory cytokines.
source: Sepsis is characterized by cytokine storm, a maladaptive response to a mismanaged infection, that is comprised of both pro- and anti-inflammatory cytokines.
evidence: Statement based on established understanding of sepsis pathophysiology

claim: Patients who survive a septic event are susceptible to unrelated secondary infection.
source: Although the acute cytokine storm is a grave situation, patients who survive a septic event are susceptible to further complications with increased susceptibility to unrelated secondary infection, increased viral reactivation, and decreased 5-year survival relative to non-septic patients (Dombrovskiy et al., 2007; Donnelly et al., 2015; Gaieski et al., 2013; Kutza et al., 1998; Walton et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: Patients who survive a septic event have increased viral reactivation.
source: Although the acute cytokine storm is a grave situation, patients who survive a septic event are susceptible to further complications with increased susceptibility to unrelated secondary infection, increased viral reactivation, and decreased 5-year survival relative to non-septic patients (Dombrovskiy et al., 2007; Donnelly et al., 2015; Gaieski et al., 2013; Kutza et al., 1998; Walton et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: Patients who survive a septic event have decreased 5-year survival relative to non-septic patients.
source: Although the acute cytokine storm is a grave situation, patients who survive a septic event are susceptible to further complications with increased susceptibility to unrelated secondary infection, increased viral reactivation, and decreased 5-year survival relative to non-septic patients (Dombrovskiy et al., 2007; Donnelly et al., 2015; Gaieski et al., 2013; Kutza et al., 1998; Walton et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: Post-sepsis complications have been attributed to the sepsis-induced lymphopenic state.
source: These factors have been attributed to the sepsis-induced lymphopenic state and functional deficits of the surviving cells (Hotchkiss et al., 2006; Hotchkiss et al., 2005; Hotchkiss et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hotchkiss et al. studies

claim: Post-sepsis complications have been attributed to functional deficits of the surviving cells.
source: These factors have been attributed to the sepsis-induced lymphopenic state and functional deficits of the surviving cells (Hotchkiss et al., 2006; Hotchkiss et al., 2005; Hotchkiss et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hotchkiss et al. studies

claim: The majority of sepsis-associated mortality has shifted to be late deaths following secondary infections or other morbid conditions as a result of immunologic impairment.
source: This state of immunoparalysis is so profound that the majority of sepsis-associated mortality has shifted to be late deaths following secondary infections or other morbid conditions as a result of immunologic impairment (Delano and Ward, 2016).
evidence: Cited from Delano and Ward, 2016

claim: Multiple sclerosis is potentially the most common non-traumatic cause of CNS disability in young adults.
source: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a chronic neuroinflammatory disease of the CNS and is potentially the most common non-traumatic cause of CNS disability in young adults (Compston and Coles, 2002).
evidence: Cited from Compston and Coles, 2002

claim: MS affects mostly women.
source: MS poses a major personal and economic burden; it effects mostly women and on average presents at age 30, an age crucial for family planning (Fox, 2004).
evidence: Cited from Fox, 2004

claim: MS on average presents at age 30.
source: MS poses a major personal and economic burden; it effects mostly women and on average presents at age 30, an age crucial for family planning (Fox, 2004).
evidence: Cited from Fox, 2004

claim: MS is thought to result from autoreactive CD4 T cell responses to the myelin antigens in the CNS followed by inflammatory cellular infiltration, demyelination, and neurodegeneration.
source: MS is thought to result from autoreactive CD4 T cell responses to the myelin antigens in the CNS followed by inflammatory cellular infiltration, demyelination, and neurodegeneration.
evidence: Statement based on established understanding of MS pathophysiology

claim: The role for CD4 T cells in EAE is well-established.
source: In experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE), a murine model of MS, this role for CD4 T cells is well-established and induced by immunization against myelin antigens (Stinissen et al., 1997).
evidence: Cited from Stinissen et al., 1997

claim: EAE is induced by immunization against myelin antigens.
source: In experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE), a murine model of MS, this role for CD4 T cells is well-established and induced by immunization against myelin antigens (Stinissen et al., 1997).
evidence: Cited from Stinissen et al., 1997

claim: Sepsis impacts both naive and memory CD4 T cells.
source: With regard to the critical role for CD4 T cells in EAE disease, the sepsis-induced lymphopenic state is known to impact both naive and memory CD4 T cells (Cabrera-Perez et al., 2016; Cabrera-Perez et al., 2015; Chen et al., 2017; Jensen et al., 2018a; Sjaastad et al., 2020b).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: Sepsis can diminish the number of naive CD4 T cell precursors subsequently limiting the number of cells capable of responding to a given antigen.
source: In particular, sepsis can diminish the number of naive CD4 T cell precursors subsequently limiting the number of cells capable of responding to a given antigen (Cabrera-Perez et al., 2015; Martin et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations

claim: Sepsis can impair the effector function of surviving T cells.
source: Additionally, sepsis can impair the effector function of surviving T cells further limiting the capacity of cells to mount an antigen-specific response (Mohr et al., 2012; Pötschke et al., 2013; Sjaastad et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations

claim: Sepsis can impair antigen-specific T cell responses through diminished number/function of dendritic cells.
source: Sepsis can also impair antigen-specific T cell responses through various cell extrinsic factors, including diminished number/function of dendritic cells (DCs) and diminished capacity of endothelial cells to promote chemotaxis (Danahy et al., 2017; Strother et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations

claim: Sepsis can impair antigen-specific T cell responses through diminished capacity of endothelial cells to promote chemotaxis.
source: Sepsis can also impair antigen-specific T cell responses through various cell extrinsic factors, including diminished number/function of dendritic cells (DCs) and diminished capacity of endothelial cells to promote chemotaxis (Danahy et al., 2017; Strother et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations

claim: CLP survivors (day 5 CLP group) had substantially diminished EAE disease severity compared to sham and no surgery control groups.
source: Importantly, while sham and no surgery control groups of mice developed robust EAE clinical disease, CLP survivors (day 5 CLP group) had substantially diminished disease severity (Figure 1b,c) and delayed disease onset (Figure 1d).
evidence: Demonstrated by clinical disease scores in Figure 1b,c

claim: CLP survivors (day 5 CLP group) had delayed EAE disease onset compared to sham and no surgery control groups.
source: Importantly, while sham and no surgery control groups of mice developed robust EAE clinical disease, CLP survivors (day 5 CLP group) had substantially diminished disease severity (Figure 1b,c) and delayed disease onset (Figure 1d).
evidence: Demonstrated by time to onset data in Figure 1d

claim: CLP hosts do not achieve similar disease severity to sham mice even when disease course is prolonged to 40 days.
source: Further, CLP hosts do not achieve similar disease severity even when disease course is prolonged (40 days) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) indicating that diminished disease is not due to delayed disease onset.
evidence: Demonstrated by extended disease monitoring in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: Diminished EAE disease in CLP hosts is not due to delayed disease onset.
source: Further, CLP hosts do not achieve similar disease severity even when disease course is prolonged (40 days) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) indicating that diminished disease is not due to delayed disease onset.
evidence: Inferred from prolonged disease monitoring showing persistent reduction in severity

claim: Day 25 CLP mice exhibited reduced disease severity relative to sham or no surgery controls.
source: Interestingly, even at this later time point CLP survivors continued to exhibit reduced disease severity (Figure 1b,c) and delayed disease onset (Figure 1d) relative to sham or no surgery controls, though disease severity was increased relative to day 5 CLP mice.
evidence: Demonstrated by clinical disease scores in Figure 1b,c

claim: Day 25 CLP mice exhibited delayed disease onset relative to sham or no surgery controls.
source: Interestingly, even at this later time point CLP survivors continued to exhibit reduced disease severity (Figure 1b,c) and delayed disease onset (Figure 1d) relative to sham or no surgery controls, though disease severity was increased relative to day 5 CLP mice.
evidence: Demonstrated by time to onset data in Figure 1d

claim: Day 25 CLP mice had increased disease severity relative to day 5 CLP mice.
source: Interestingly, even at this later time point CLP survivors continued to exhibit reduced disease severity (Figure 1b,c) and delayed disease onset (Figure 1d) relative to sham or no surgery controls, though disease severity was increased relative to day 5 CLP mice.
evidence: Demonstrated by comparison of disease scores in Figure 1b,c

claim: The more severe disease in day 25 CLP mice relative to day 5 mice was due to noted variability among the day 25 CLP mice, wherein some individuals developed severe disease and others had minimal disease.
source: The more severe disease relative to day 5 mice was due to a noted variability among the day 25 CLP mice, wherein some individuals developed severe disease and others had minimal disease.
evidence: Observation of variability in disease outcomes

claim: The influence of the immunoparalysis state may wane with time.
source: This difference in EAE severity suggests that the influence of the immunoparalysis state may wain with time, at least in some of the mice.
evidence: Inferred from the variability in disease severity at day 25

claim: CLP mice with EAE had less CNS pathology as highlighted by reduced inflammatory cell infiltrate in both the parenchyma and meninges of the spinal cord.
source: Corresponding with their milder disease, CLP mice with EAE had less CNS pathology as highlighted by reduced inflammatory cell infiltrate (Figure 1e,H and E) in both the parenchyma (Figure 1f) and meninges (Figure 1g) of the spinal cord, the primary target of EAE inflammation.
evidence: Demonstrated by histopathologic scoring in Figure 1e-g

claim: CLP mice had milder axonal demyelination.
source: Further, CLP mice had milder axonal demyelination (Figure 1e, LFB) and vacuole formation, factors associated with EAE-induced paralysis.
evidence: Demonstrated by LFB staining in Figure 1e

claim: CLP mice had milder vacuole formation.
source: Further, CLP mice had milder axonal demyelination (Figure 1e, LFB) and vacuole formation, factors associated with EAE-induced paralysis.
evidence: Demonstrated by histology in Figure 1e

claim: Axonal demyelination and vacuole formation are factors associated with EAE-induced paralysis.
source: Further, CLP mice had milder axonal demyelination (Figure 1e, LFB) and vacuole formation, factors associated with EAE-induced paralysis.
evidence: Statement based on established understanding of EAE pathology

claim: CLP hosts had a reduced frequency and number of both microglia and infiltrating monocytes and macrophages present within the CNS.
source: The difference in infiltrate observed extended to a reduced frequency and number of both microglia and infiltrating monocytes and macrophages present within the CNS in CLP hosts, relative to their sham counterparts (Figure 1—figure supplement 3a–e).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry in Figure 1—figure supplement 3a-e

claim: A significant reduction in MHC II expression was observed on both microglia and infiltrating monocytes/macrophages in CLP hosts compared to sham-treated mice.
source: A significant reduction in MHC II expression was also observed on both microglia and infiltrating monocytes/macrophages in CLP hosts compared to sham-treated mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 3f,h).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry in Figure 1—figure supplement 3f,h

claim: The reduction in MHC II expression compounded with the reduced number of myeloid cells led to ~100 fold reduction in MHC II-expressing cells in CLP hosts.
source: This reduction compounded with the already reduced number of myeloid cells leading to ~100 fold reduction in MHC II-expressing cells in CLP hosts (Figure 1—figure supplement 3g,i).
evidence: Calculated from flow cytometry data in Figure 1—figure supplement 3g,i

claim: MHC II expression is a marker of activation of myeloid cell populations.
source: MHC II expression is not only a marker of activation of these cell populations but also serves to present antigen to CD4 T cells, including autoreactive T cells that are critical mediators of disease in EAE.
evidence: Statement based on established immunological knowledge

claim: MHC II serves to present antigen to CD4 T cells, including autoreactive T cells that are critical mediators of disease in EAE.
source: MHC II expression is not only a marker of activation of these cell populations but also serves to present antigen to CD4 T cells, including autoreactive T cells that are critical mediators of disease in EAE.
evidence: Statement based on established immunological knowledge

claim: Flow cytometric analysis of the CNS revealed a decreased frequency and number of antigen-experienced CD4+ CD11a+ cells in the CNS of CLP hosts.
source: Flow cytometric analysis of the CNS revealed a decreased frequency (Figure 2b,c) and number (Figure 2d) of antigen-experienced CD4+ CD11a+ cells in the CNS (Christiaansen et al., 2017).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry in Figure 2b-d

claim: Tetramer staining of CD4 T cells reactive to the MOG antigen revealed a reduction in the frequency and number of this pathogenic effector population in CLP hosts.
source: Further, tetramer staining of CD4 T cells reactive to the MOG antigen revealed a further reduction in the frequency (Figure 2e,f) and number (Figure 2g) of this pathogenic effector population.
evidence: Demonstrated by tetramer staining in Figure 2e-g

claim: No differences were observed in the frequencies of MOG-specific CD4 T cells producing pathogenic effector cytokines IFNγ, IL-17A, and TNFα without further stimulation directly ex vivo between sham and CLP hosts.
source: No differences were observed in the frequencies of MOG-specific CD4 T cells producing pathogenic effector cytokines IFNγ, IL-17A, and TNFα without further stimulation directly ex vivo (Figure 3a,b; Figure 3—figure supplement 1; Lee et al., 2019).
evidence: Demonstrated by intracellular cytokine staining in Figure 3a,b

claim: The numerical deficit in MOG-specific CD4 T cells led to a significant reduction in the number of IFNγ- and TNFα-producing cells.
source: However, the numerical deficit in MOG-specific CD4 T cells led to a significant reduction in the number of IFNγ- and TNFα-producing cells with a trending decrease in IL-17A-producing cells (Figure 3c).
evidence: Demonstrated by cell counts in Figure 3c

claim: The numerical deficit in MOG-specific CD4 T cells led to a trending decrease in IL-17A-producing cells.
source: However, the numerical deficit in MOG-specific CD4 T cells led to a significant reduction in the number of IFNγ- and TNFα-producing cells with a trending decrease in IL-17A-producing cells (Figure 3c).
evidence: Demonstrated by cell counts in Figure 3c

claim: The autoantigen-specific CD4 T cells present in the CNS after CLP surgery are functionally competent.
source: This finding indicates the autoantigen-specific CD4 T cells present in the CNS after CLP surgery are functionally competent and potentially were the least impacted by the septic event.
evidence: Inferred from equivalent cytokine production frequencies

claim: Both the frequency and number of MOG-specific CD4 T cells were decreased in the iLN of CLP hosts at day 7 after EAE induction.
source: Similar to the CNS during peak disease, both the frequency (Figure 4b) and number (Figure 4c) of MOG-specific CD4 T cells were decreased in the iLN of CLP hosts.
evidence: Demonstrated by tetramer staining in Figure 4b,c

claim: Tetramer enrichment analysis revealed a significant numerical loss of MOG-specific CD4 T cell precursors in CLP hosts 5 days after surgery.
source: This analysis revealed a significant numerical loss of MOG-specific CD4 T cell precursors in CLP hosts.
evidence: Demonstrated by tetramer enrichment in Figure 5

claim: An increased frequency of activated (CD44hi) CD4 T cells was observed in CLP hosts.
source: Additionally, similar to prior reports (Cabrera-Perez et al., 2016; Jensen et al., 2018a; Skirecki et al., 2020), an increased frequency of activated (CD44hi) CD4 T cells was observed in CLP hosts (Figure 5e).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry in Figure 5e and supported by citations

claim: An increase in the frequency of memory-like CD44hi cells among MOG-specific CD4 T cells was observed in CLP hosts.
source: Importantly, this extended to an increase in the frequency of memory-like CD44hi cells among MOG-specific CD4 T cells in CLP hosts (Figure 5f).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry in Figure 5f

claim: 2D2 cells that were transferred prior to surgery were numerically diminished in CLP hosts relative to sham counterparts.
source: Notably, cells that were transferred prior to surgery were numerically diminished in CLP hosts relative to sham counterparts (Figure 6c) recapitulating the observations with endogenous MOG-specific CD4 T cells (see Figure 5).
evidence: Demonstrated by cell counts in Figure 6c

claim: 2D2 cells that were transferred after surgery were numerically equivalent between sham and CLP hosts.
source: Strikingly, 2D2 cells that were transferred after surgery were numerically equivalent between sham and CLP hosts, suggesting the septic environment (e.g. diminished DC number/function, increased proportion of regulatory CD8 and/or CD4 T cells) did not limit their capacity to expand (Figure 6c).
evidence: Demonstrated by cell counts in Figure 6c

claim: The septic environment did not limit the capacity of post-transfer 2D2 cells to expand.
source: Strikingly, 2D2 cells that were transferred after surgery were numerically equivalent between sham and CLP hosts, suggesting the septic environment (e.g. diminished DC number/function, increased proportion of regulatory CD8 and/or CD4 T cells) did not limit their capacity to expand (Figure 6c).
evidence: Inferred from equivalent cell numbers in post-transfer groups

claim: The transferred 2D2 cells from all groups had a similar proportion of recently proliferated cells.
source: Further, the transferred 2D2 cells from all groups had a similar proportion of recently proliferated as well as apoptotic (FLICA+ PI+) cells (Figure 6d,e).
evidence: Demonstrated by Ki67 staining in Figure 6d

claim: The transferred 2D2 cells from all groups had a similar proportion of apoptotic (FLICA+ PI+) cells.
source: Further, the transferred 2D2 cells from all groups had a similar proportion of recently proliferated as well as apoptotic (FLICA+ PI+) cells (Figure 6d,e).
evidence: Demonstrated by FLICA/PI staining in Figure 6e

claim: Autoantigen CD4 T cells are not limited by the post-septic environment in their capacity to be primed and expand.
source: Given that the post-transfer groups had equivalent cell numbers, proliferation, and apoptosis; these data demonstrate that autoantigen CD4 T cells are not limited by the post-septic environment in their capacity to be primed and expand.
evidence: Inferred from equivalent expansion of post-transfer 2D2 cells

claim: There was no observed difference in the expression of Fas, FasL, and TRAIL between sham and CLP hosts for either the pre- or post-transfer groups.
source: In addition, there was no observed difference in the expression of several canonical extrinsic death-inducing proteins known to limit the expansion of CD4 T cells (i.e. Fas, FasL, TRAIL) between sham and CLP hosts for either the pre- or post-transfer groups (Figure 6—figure supplement 1) further supporting the notion that survival differences do not account for the numerical deficit in CD4 T cells exposed to sepsis.
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry in Figure 6—figure supplement 1

claim: Survival differences do not account for the numerical deficit in CD4 T cells exposed to sepsis.
source: In addition, there was no observed difference in the expression of several canonical extrinsic death-inducing proteins known to limit the expansion of CD4 T cells (i.e. Fas, FasL, TRAIL) between sham and CLP hosts for either the pre- or post-transfer groups (Figure 6—figure supplement 1) further supporting the notion that survival differences do not account for the numerical deficit in CD4 T cells exposed to sepsis.
evidence: Inferred from equivalent death marker expression

claim: Pre-transfer 2D2 cells proliferate and die equivalently in both sham and CLP hosts.
source: Therefore, pre-transfer 2D2 cells proliferate and die equivalently in both sham and CLP hosts, indicating that sepsis does not intrinsically impair the capacity of these cells to proliferate in response to cognate antigen recognition.
evidence: Inferred from equivalent proliferation and apoptosis markers

claim: Sepsis does not intrinsically impair the capacity of 2D2 cells to proliferate in response to cognate antigen recognition.
source: Therefore, pre-transfer 2D2 cells proliferate and die equivalently in both sham and CLP hosts, indicating that sepsis does not intrinsically impair the capacity of these cells to proliferate in response to cognate antigen recognition.
evidence: Inferred from equivalent proliferation of pre-transfer 2D2 cells

claim: No difference was observed in either the survival or expansion potential of 2D2 cells acquired from CLP mice relative to those acquired from sham controls.
source: Importantly, no difference was observed in either the survival or expansion potential of 2D2 cells acquired from CLP mice relative to those acquired from sham controls (Figure 7b,c).
evidence: Demonstrated by competitive transfer experiment in Figure 7b,c

claim: CLP does not change the capacity of autoantigen-specific CD4 T cells to exert their effector function(s) upon transfer into a non-septic environment.
source: Thus, these data demonstrate that CLP does not change the capacity of autoantigen-specific CD4 T cells to exert their effector function(s) upon transfer into a non-septic environment.
evidence: Inferred from equivalent survival and expansion in competitive transfer

claim: Mice that received 2D2 CD4 T cells prior to surgery developed less severe disease than their sham counterparts.
source: Coinciding with the cellular expansion seen in the iLN, mice that received 2D2 CD4 T cells prior to surgery developed less severe disease than their sham counterparts (Figure 8b,c), similar to results in Figure 1.
evidence: Demonstrated by disease scores in Figure 8b,c

claim: CLP mice that received 2D2 CD4 T cells post-surgery developed equivalent disease as sham counterparts.
source: However, CLP mice that received 2D2 CD4 T cells post-surgery developed equivalent disease as sham counterparts (Figure 8b,c).
evidence: Demonstrated by disease scores in Figure 8b,c

claim: A determining factor by which sepsis limits EAE stems from a reduction in number of naive MOG-specific CD4 T cell precursors.
source: This result demonstrates that a determining factor by which sepsis limits EAE stems from a reduction in number of naive MOG-specific CD4 T cell precursors.
evidence: Inferred from rescue of disease by post-transfer of 2D2 cells

claim: There was a numerical reduction in the CNS infiltration of both transferred 2D2 and endogenous MOG-specific CD4 T cells of CLP mice that received transfer prior to surgery.
source: Importantly, there was a numerical reduction in the CNS infiltration of both transferred 2D2 (Figure 8d) and endogenous MOG-specific CD4 T cells (Figure 8f) of CLP mice that received transfer prior to surgery demonstrating that both populations of cells were similarly influenced by the septic event.
evidence: Demonstrated by CNS cell counts in Figure 8d,f

claim: There was not a numerical deficit in 2D2 CD4 T cells when transferred into CLP hosts post-surgery.
source: Conversely, there was not a numerical deficit in 2D2 CD4 T cells when transferred into CLP hosts post-surgery (Figure 8e), while the number of endogenous MOG-specific CD4 T cells in the CNS in the same hosts were significantly reduced (Figure 8g).
evidence: Demonstrated by CNS cell counts in Figure 8e

claim: The number of endogenous MOG-specific CD4 T cells in the CNS of post-transfer CLP hosts were significantly reduced.
source: Conversely, there was not a numerical deficit in 2D2 CD4 T cells when transferred into CLP hosts post-surgery (Figure 8e), while the number of endogenous MOG-specific CD4 T cells in the CNS in the same hosts were significantly reduced (Figure 8g).
evidence: Demonstrated by CNS cell counts in Figure 8g

claim: Numerical loss, due to sepsis-induced lymphopenia, of naive autoantigen-specific CD4 T cell precursors is sufficient to explain the protective effect of CLP on EAE disease.
source: Cumulatively, these data indicate that numerical loss, due to sepsis-induced lymphopenia, of naive autoantigen-specific CD4 T cell precursors is sufficient to explain the protective effect of CLP on EAE disease.
evidence: Inferred from the complete rescue of disease by post-transfer of 2D2 cells

claim: Following cecal ligation and puncture (CLP), mice have diminished EAE disease severity.
source: Herein, we demonstrate that following cecal ligation and puncture (CLP), mice have diminished EAE disease severity.
evidence: Summary of experimental findings

claim: Autoantigen-specific effector CD4 T cells were reduced in CLP hosts with EAE due to a loss of their naive precursors.
source: Autoantigen-specific effector CD4 T cells were reduced in CLP hosts with EAE due to a loss of their naive precursors, which was the determining factor in the impediment of EAE disease.
evidence: Summary of experimental findings

claim: The loss of naive precursors was the determining factor in the impediment of EAE disease.
source: Autoantigen-specific effector CD4 T cells were reduced in CLP hosts with EAE due to a loss of their naive precursors, which was the determining factor in the impediment of EAE disease.
evidence: Summary of experimental findings

claim: Sepsis diminishes the number of MOG-specific CD4 T cell precursors but does not alter capacity of the surviving cells to proliferate.
source: With these tools, we established that sepsis diminishes the number of MOG-specific CD4 T cell precursors but does not alter capacity of the surviving cells to proliferate (either by intrinsic or extrinsic mechanisms) or promote disease if numerically bolstered.
evidence: Summary of experimental findings from 2D2 transfer experiments

claim: Sepsis does not alter capacity of surviving MOG-specific CD4 T cells to promote disease if numerically bolstered.
source: With these tools, we established that sepsis diminishes the number of MOG-specific CD4 T cell precursors but does not alter capacity of the surviving cells to proliferate (either by intrinsic or extrinsic mechanisms) or promote disease if numerically bolstered.
evidence: Summary of experimental findings from 2D2 transfer experiments

claim: The number of MOG-specific naive CD4 T cell precursors is a critical determining factor in the development of EAE disease.
source: In the context of EAE, our findings suggest that the number of MOG-specific naive CD4 T cell precursors is a critical determining factor in the development of disease.
evidence: Inferred from rescue experiments with 2D2 transfers

claim: Allelic differences in HLA-expression may influence the development of MS by differential generation of autoreactive naive CD4 T cells.
source: Specifically, allelic differences in HLA-expression may influence the development of MS by differential generation of autoreactive naive CD4 T cells (Patsopoulos, 2018).
evidence: Cited from Patsopoulos, 2018

claim: Environmental factors can influence the precursor frequency by influencing central tolerance (i.e. vitamin-D-regulated HLA DRB1*1501 expression).
source: Environmental factors can also influence the precursor frequency either by influencing central tolerance (i.e. vitamin-D-regulated HLA DRB1*1501 expression) or peripheral tolerance (i.e. gut-microbe-regulated Treg frequency and function) (Freedman et al., 2018; Ramagopalan et al., 2009).
evidence: Cited from Freedman et al., 2018 and Ramagopalan et al., 2009

claim: Environmental factors can influence the precursor frequency by influencing peripheral tolerance (i.e. gut-microbe-regulated Treg frequency and function).
source: Environmental factors can also influence the precursor frequency either by influencing central tolerance (i.e. vitamin-D-regulated HLA DRB1*1501 expression) or peripheral tolerance (i.e. gut-microbe-regulated Treg frequency and function) (Freedman et al., 2018; Ramagopalan et al., 2009).
evidence: Cited from Freedman et al., 2018 and Ramagopalan et al., 2009

claim: It is plausible that sepsis can modulate the development of MS and/or disease relapses.
source: As antigen-specific CD4+ T cell responses play a significant role in the pathogenesis of MS, it is plausible that sepsis can modulate the development of MS and/or disease relapses.
evidence: Speculative inference based on EAE findings

claim: There are no clinical data on the effect of sepsis on the disease development or relapses in patients with MS.
source: However, there are no clinical data on the effect of sepsis on the disease development or relapses in patients with MS.
evidence: Statement of absence of clinical data

claim: A numerical recovery of MOG-specific CD4 T cells with time after sepsis was observed in some animals.
source: Additionally, we observed a numerical recovery of MOG-specific CD4 T cells with time after sepsis in some animals.
evidence: Observation from day 25 experiments

claim: The recovered MOG-specific CD4s from CLP hosts may exhibit inherent differences from MOG-specific CD4s within sham counterparts.
source: Yet, the recovered MOG-specific CD4s from CLP hosts may still exhibit inherent differences from MOG-specific CD4s within sham counterparts (e.g. potential reduced avidity of 'recovered' cells).
evidence: Speculation based on observed phenotypic differences

claim: The acquisition of an antigen-experienced phenotype by MOG-specific CD4 T cells from CLP mice demonstrates a functional difference that may influence the function of these CD4 T cells.
source: Indeed, the acquisition of an antigen-experienced phenotype by MOG-specific CD4 T cells from CLP mice demonstrates one such difference that may influence the function of these CD4 T cells.
evidence: Inferred from CD44 expression data

claim: Auto-reactive T cells from MS patients have increased survival capacity.
source: Auto-reactive T cells from MS patients have several functional differences, including increased survival capacity, distinct transcriptomic profiles, and increased avidity for autoantigen (Bieganowska et al., 1997; Bielekova et al., 2004; Cao et al., 2015; Hong et al., 2004).
evidence: Cited from multiple references

claim: Auto-reactive T cells from MS patients have distinct transcriptomic profiles.
source: Auto-reactive T cells from MS patients have several functional differences, including increased survival capacity, distinct transcriptomic profiles, and increased avidity for autoantigen (Bieganowska et al., 1997; Bielekova et al., 2004; Cao et al., 2015; Hong et al., 2004).
evidence: Cited from multiple references

claim: Auto-reactive T cells from MS patients have increased avidity for autoantigen.
source: Auto-reactive T cells from MS patients have several functional differences, including increased survival capacity, distinct transcriptomic profiles, and increased avidity for autoantigen (Bieganowska et al., 1997; Bielekova et al., 2004; Cao et al., 2015; Hong et al., 2004).
evidence: Cited from multiple references

claim: Some CD4 T cell precursors eventually recover to pre-sepsis numbers with time, whereas others remain numerically decreased or can even be numerically expanded.
source: However, previous work has described how some CD4 T cell precursors eventually recover to pre-sepsis numbers with time, whereas others remain numerically decreased or can even be numerically expanded (Cabrera-Perez et al., 2015).
evidence: Cited from Cabrera-Perez et al., 2015

claim: T cells that expand via homeostatic proliferation in lymphopenic states can gain an antigen-experienced phenotype and effector function.
source: Further, T cells that expand via homeostatic proliferation in lymphopenic states, such as the post-septic environment, can gain an antigen-experienced phenotype and effector function (Hamilton et al., 2006).
evidence: Cited from Hamilton et al., 2006

claim: CD4 Tregs are more resistant to sepsis-induced numerical loss than other CD4 T cell subsets.
